tip: The number dau (two) soft-mutates the next noun: cwpanaid becomes gwpanaid. ddau gwpanaid o de = two cups of tea.
mewn means 'in' before an indefinite noun: mewn tair awr = in three hours. Use yn only before a definite noun.
The passive uses cael plus a possessive: ei werthu, literally 'its selling'. Cafodd... ei werthu = it was sold.
Welsh needs no word for 'to' between two verbs: Dysgodd hi siarad = she learned to speak. siarad stays plain.
Reported questions keep statement order, with mae straight after pam: pam mae'r awyr yn las = why the sky is blue.
A past-tense verb's object soft-mutates: cinio becomes ginio. Coginiodd Nerys ginio = Nerys cooked lunch.
After beth (what) a verb soft-mutates: digwyddodd becomes ddigwyddodd. beth ddigwyddodd = what happened.
Feminine nouns soft-mutate after y or 'r (the): cegin becomes gegin. Paentiodd e'r gegin = he painted the kitchen.
torth is feminine, so 'three' is tair not tri, here mutated to dair: dair torth = three loaves.
Dylai means 'should' or 'ought to': Dylai fe ymddiheuro = he should apologise. It has no plain past form.
syrthio i gysgu is the set phrase for 'fall asleep', literally 'fall to sleep': Syrthiodd e i gysgu.
i before a verb shows purpose: i adael = in order to let. Agorodd hi'r ffenest i adael awyr = opened it to let air.
yn plus a verbnoun renders '-ing' after verbs of perception: y plant yn chwerthin = the children laughing.
Welsh past tense keeps Verb-Subject-Object order: Derbyniodd e'r cynnig = he accepted the offer, verb first.
A noun stays singular after a number: bum milltir = five miles, not a plural. pump shortens to bum here.
Report 'that' with a bod form: Cwynodd hi fod y gwasanaeth yn wael = she complained that the service was poor.
Object pronouns follow the verb and subject: Gwahododd nhw ni = they invited us. nhw is subject, ni object.
Clock times use o'r gloch, literally 'of the bell': am wyth o'r gloch = at eight o'clock. am marks 'at'.
Adjectives soft-mutate after a feminine noun: cyntaf becomes gyntaf. y wobr gyntaf = the first prize.
'On a day' is shown by a soft mutation, with no word for 'on': dydd becomes ddydd. ddydd Sul = on Sunday.
can (hundred) triggers a nasal mutation on the next word: blwydd becomes mlwydd. saith can mlwydd oed = 700 years old.
ei meaning 'his' soft-mutates the next word: dwylo becomes ddwylo. ei ddwylo = his hands.
Wrap 'our' around the noun for emphasis: ein tîm ni = our team, with ni echoing the possessive ein.
'Was born' is Cafodd plus a possessive plus geni, literally 'got their birth': Cafodd hi ei geni = she was born.
ei meaning 'her' aspirate-mutates p, t, c: tad-cu becomes thad-cu. ei thad-cu = her grandfather.
The feminine ei (her, its) aspirate-mutates p, t, c: pobi becomes phobi. y gacen... ei phobi = the cake was baked.
a marks a relative clause meaning 'who' or 'which': Y ferch a enillodd y fedal = the girl who won the medal.
a (and) aspirate-mutates only the very next word if it starts p, t or c: caws becomes chaws. bara a chaws.
dod (to come) is irregular in the past: daeth = came, not 'dododd'. Daeth ei rhieni = her parents came.
Some verbs need a fixed preposition: sylwi ar = to notice, literally 'notice on'. Sylwodd e... ar y camgymeriad.
pêl is feminine, so it soft-mutates after 'r: Taflodd e'r bêl = he threw the ball, from pêl.
i (to) soft-mutates a place name: Caerdydd becomes Gaerdydd. i Gaerdydd = to Cardiff.
pan (when) soft-mutates the verb after it: cnociodd becomes gnociodd. pan gnociodd = when someone knocked.
Negatives soft-mutate the verb and add ddim: Ddwedodd hi ddim = she did not say, from dwedodd.
Possession is two nouns side by side, with no 'of': brawd fy ffrind = my friend's brother.
siarad â means 'to speak to': Siaradodd hi â'r athro = she spoke to the teacher. â marks who is addressed.
Prepositions take personal endings: heb (without) plus 'me' becomes hebdda i = without me.
Report 'that he' with ei fod e: Mynnodd e ei fod e'n iawn = he insisted that he was right.
mynd â means 'to take', literally 'go with': Aeth Megan â'r plant = Megan took the children.
mynd (to go) is irregular in the past: aeth = went, not 'mynddodd'. Aeth y bachgen = the boy went.
a (and) aspirate-mutates the next verb: prynu becomes phrynu. Aeth Owain... a phrynu = went and bought.
Roeddwn i'n plus a verb is the background action; a short past-tense verb interrupts it: darllen... pan aeth = reading when it went out.
heb i (someone) means 'without them doing something': heb iddo sylwi = without him noticing.
cyn i (someone) soft-mutates the verb: coginio becomes goginio. cyn iddi goginio = before she cooked.
Welsh has no verb 'to have'; possession uses gan: Roedd llais hyfryd ganddi = she had a lovely voice.
South Welsh shows possession with gyda: beiro gyda ti = you have a pen, literally 'a pen with you'.
Ga i...? asks 'may I have...?' and soft-mutates the noun: paned becomes baned. Ga i baned o de?
Alli di...? means 'can you...?' and soft-mutates the verb: pasio becomes basio. Alli di basio'r halen?
Dylwn i means 'I should' and soft-mutates the verb: bwyta becomes fwyta. Dylwn i fwyta = I should eat.
Rhaid i (someone) means 'must', and the verb soft-mutates: cymryd becomes gymryd. Rhaid iddi hi gymryd = she must take.
Arferai means 'used to' and soft-mutates the verb: cerdded becomes gerdded. Arferai hi gerdded = she used to walk.
eisiau (to want) takes no yn linker: Wyt ti eisiau bisgïen? = do you want a biscuit, never 'wyt ti'n eisiau'.
Here a means 'whether' in an indirect question: Gofynnodd e... a oeddwn i = he asked whether I was.
Front the key word for emphasis: Cymraeg dw i eisiau dysgu = it is Welsh I want to learn, stressing Cymraeg.
na before a consonant, nag before a vowel: cryfach nag ydw i = stronger than I am. Like English a and an.
'As...as' is mor plus adjective plus â, or ag before a vowel: mor brydferth ag eos = as beautiful as a nightingale.
Pe bai sets up an unreal 'if': Pe bai'r plant yn dawel = if the children were quiet, implying they are not.
heb plus a verbnoun is the 'not done yet' half of the perfect: heb ei bostio = without having posted it.
roedd plus wedi means 'had done', the pluperfect: Roeddwn i wedi anghofio = I had forgotten.
